script.opening: "I keep getting crampy pain low down on the left side of my tummy, and my bowels are all over the place — constipated then loose. A scan a while back mentioned diverticular disease. Is that what’s causing it, and what do I do about it?"

facts.text: On and off for about 4 months. Crampy, low on the left, comes and goes, eases after opening her bowels. Not constant. No fever.
"It isn’t how my bowels used to be." For about 4 months: a few days constipated, then loose for a day or two. Used to be regular once a day. Some bloating.
No blood she has seen, no black stools. Weight steady, "feel all right in myself". Not tired or breathless. No lumps. No vomiting. No air or faeces in the urine. No family history of bowel cancer.
If asked about examinations: saw the out-of-hours GP 3 weeks ago during a bad spell: "He said my temperature was normal, my tummy was soft and a bit tender low on the left, and there were no lumps."

"I’m not sure what kind of scan it was." A CT for kidney-stone pain 2 years ago that "mentioned diverticular disease". Never had a camera test of the bowel. Not sure she has done the home bowel screening kit — "I think I threw the last one away".
Just paracetamol now and then. Takes no ibuprofen. No allergies. Blood pressure "fine". Non-smoker; a glass of wine at weekends. Diet: white bread, not much fruit or veg.
Retired school secretary. Married, two grown-up children. Plans days out around toilets lately.

Pleasant, matter-of-fact. You assume the diverticular disease explains everything. If cancer is raised calmly, be surprised but accept the test: "Cancer? I hadn’t even thought of that." Ask whether you need antibiotics.

ice.concerns: "I just want to know how to stop the pain and get my bowels back to normal."
ice.expectations: "A plan to sort the pain — maybe antibiotics."

cues: "It isn’t how my bowels used to be" — a change in bowel habit needing FIT.
"I don’t remember a camera test" — the colon has not been examined.
"I threw the last screening kit away" (if asked) — missed bowel screening.

checkpoints.text: Distinguishes DIVERTICULOSIS (asymptomatic, incidental — fibre/lifestyle only), symptomatic DIVERTICULAR DISEASE (intermittent LIF colicky pain/altered habit), and acute DIVERTICULITIS (constant LIF pain, fever, tenderness, raised markers)

Manages symptomatic diverticular disease conservatively per NICE NG147 (high fibre/fluids, lifestyle, manage constipation, bulk-forming laxatives, antispasmodics, paracetamol not NSAIDs/opioids, no antibiotics)

Recognises acute diverticulitis and its management (uncomplicated and systemically well — consider a no-antibiotic strategy; co-amoxiclav if systemically unwell/high-risk, NICE NG147; same-day hospital for complications)
Recognises and safety-nets COMPLICATIONS/red flags needing urgent admission (peritonism, sepsis, significant PR bleeding, perforation/abscess, obstruction)

Does NOT assume "just diverticular disease" — offers FIT now for the change in bowel habit (NICE NG12 and HTG690; suspected cancer pathway referral if 10 µg Hb/g or more), asks whether the earlier scan examined the colon, and screens other red flags (bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, mass)
Explains the diagnosis and management clearly, reassures appropriately, and checks understanding

Explains calmly why a bowel cancer check is advised (she has not raised it herself) and the difference between harmless diverticulosis and features to watch for in clear language, agreeing the FIT and safety-net plan with her

Safety-nets and follows up: complication/diverticulitis red flags warranting urgent assessment/admission, FIT now with a suspected cancer pathway referral if positive, fibre/lifestyle, and review — managing diverticular disease while not missing colorectal cancer

worked.txt: "Diverticular disease means small pouches in the bowel wall. Often they cause no symptoms, but they can give exactly what you describe — crampy left-sided pain and unpredictable bowels. That’s the symptomatic form, and it’s manageable."

"The mainstays are building up fibre gradually, plenty of fluids, staying active, keeping your bowels regular with a fibre supplement, and a medicine to ease the cramps if needed. Keep to paracetamol for pain and avoid anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen. That settles things for most people."

"Sometimes a pouch gets inflamed — diverticulitis — with more constant pain on the left, a fever and tenderness. That needs assessing — mild cases often settle without antibiotics, which are for when someone is unwell with infection — and occasionally hospital."

"Get urgent help if you have severe tummy pain with a hard, very tender belly, a high fever, significant bleeding from the back passage, or you can’t pass anything and are vomiting — those are emergencies."

"Importantly, I won’t just put everything down to diverticular disease — because bowel cancer can cause similar symptoms or occur alongside it. At 62, a change in bowel habit is a reason to check, so I’d like you to do a simple home stool test (FIT) now, and if it’s positive I’ll refer you urgently for a camera test. Do you know what the earlier scan was — a CT, or a camera test into the bowel?"

"Let’s start the fibre and lifestyle approach, and do the FIT and blood tests now. Even if the FIT is normal, come back if the symptoms continue, and seek help the same day if you notice bleeding, or the pain becomes constant, severe or feverish."

f.learning: DIVERTICULAR DISEASE spans a spectrum that must be distinguished: DIVERTICULOSIS (asymptomatic pouches, often an incidental finding — no treatment needed beyond fibre/lifestyle); symptomatic DIVERTICULAR DISEASE (intermittent left lower-quadrant colicky pain, altered bowel habit, bloating — managed conservatively per NICE NG147 with a high-fibre diet, adequate fluids, lifestyle, management of constipation, bulk-forming laxatives and antispasmodics for pain, paracetamol rather than NSAIDs/opioids, and no antibiotics); and acute DIVERTICULITIS (inflammation — constant LIF pain, fever, localised tenderness/guarding, raised CRP/WCC), where uncomplicated cases in a systemically well person may be managed in primary care with a no-antibiotic strategy (co-amoxiclav if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or comorbid — NICE NG147) with review, but admission is needed for systemic illness/sepsis, significant pain/peritonism, complications, immunosuppression or inability to cope at home. Recognise and safety-net the COMPLICATIONS/red flags needing urgent admission: severe pain/peritonism, high fever/sepsis, significant PR bleeding/haemorrhage, perforation/abscess, and obstruction (vomiting, distension, absolute constipation). Crucially, do NOT attribute all bowel symptoms to "just diverticular disease", because COLORECTAL CANCER can mimic or coexist — a change in bowel habit is itself a FIT criterion under NICE NG12 and HTG690 (as are an abdominal mass, iron-deficiency anaemia, and age-based rectal bleeding, pain or weight-loss criteria), so offer FIT now and make a suspected cancer pathway referral if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more, remembering that a normal FIT does not end the matter if symptoms persist and that an earlier CT reporting diverticula may not have examined the colon for a tumour. The skill is distinguishing diverticulosis/disease/diverticulitis, managing appropriately, safety-netting complications, and not missing colorectal cancer. NICE NG12 lower-GI applies where red flags are present.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG147 Diverticular disease: diagnosis and management (2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE HTG690 Quantitative faecal immunochemical testing to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care · [4] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over
knowledge.summary: Diverticulosis is common and usually incidental; diverticular disease means symptoms from the diverticula; diverticulitis means inflammation. A 62-year-old with a change in bowel habit must not have it written off as diverticular disease: NICE NG12 and HTG690 [2, 3] recommend offering FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit, and a result of 10 µg Hb/g or more triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral. Manage the symptomatic disease with diet, fluids, bulk-forming laxatives and an antispasmodic [1]; recognise acute diverticulitis and its complications, and give clear safety-net advice.

points.t: Diverticulosis: pouches without symptoms, usually found incidentally. Diverticular disease: intermittent lower abdominal (usually left-sided) pain, often with altered bowel habit, bloating or mucus, without systemic inflammation. Acute diverticulitis: constant abdominal pain, usually left iliac fossa, with fever, localised tenderness and raised inflammatory markers; complicated if abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction or haemorrhage [1].

NG147 [1]: advise a healthy balanced diet with whole grains, fruit and vegetables, increasing fibre gradually with adequate fluids; consider a bulk-forming laxative for constipation and an antispasmodic for cramping; do not offer antibiotics for diverticular disease. Doses per BNF. Review NSAID and opioid use, which are linked to complications.

NG147 [1]: if systemically well without complications, consider a no-antibiotic strategy with advice to return if symptoms persist or worsen; offer an antibiotic (co-amoxiclav first choice, per NG147 and BNF) if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or with significant comorbidity. Advise paracetamol and avoidance of NSAIDs and opioids where possible, because they may increase the risk of perforation. Refer for same-day hospital assessment if pain is uncontrolled, a complication is suspected, fluids cannot be maintained, or the person is frail or cannot be managed at home.

NICE NG12 [2] and HTG690 [3]: offer FIT to adults with an abdominal mass, a change in bowel habit or iron-deficiency anaemia; to those aged 40 and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain; to those under 50 with rectal bleeding and unexplained abdominal pain or weight loss; to those aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss; and to those aged 60 and over with anaemia even without iron deficiency. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more. A rectal mass or unexplained anal mass or ulceration is referred without FIT. A normal FIT does not end the matter if symptoms persist.

Find out what the earlier scan was and whether the whole colon was examined. A CT that reported diverticula is not the same as a colonoscopy or CT colonography that excluded a tumour, and symptoms may have changed since.

Severe or generalised abdominal pain or peritonism, sepsis features [4], significant rectal bleeding, vomiting with distension and absolute constipation (obstruction), pneumaturia or faecal vaginal discharge (fistula), or failure to improve. These need same-day hospital assessment.

model.text: Hello Mrs Carver, I’m Dr Clarke. What’s been happening?

I keep getting crampy pain low down on the left side of my tummy, and my bowels are all over the place: constipated, then loose. A scan a while back mentioned diverticular disease. Is that what’s causing it, and what do I do about it?
Thank you. It may well be, but I want to make sure we’re not missing anything else, so I’ll ask a few questions and go through the examination recorded earlier.
model.why: Signals that diverticular disease will not be assumed

model.text: When did the change in your bowels start, and is it different from what’s normal for you?
model.why: Establishes a change in bowel habit: an NICE NG12 FIT criterion

model.text: It’s been going on a while now. It isn’t how my bowels used to be.
Have you noticed any blood from your back passage, mixed in or on the paper, or black stools?
No, I haven’t seen any.
Any weight loss without trying, loss of appetite, or feeling unusually tired or breathless?
model.why: Weight loss and symptoms of anaemia

model.text: I don’t think I’ve lost weight, and I feel all right in myself.
Tell me about the pain. Does it come and go, or has it ever been constant, with a fever or feeling shivery and unwell?
It comes and goes. Cramps, then it eases, especially after I open my bowels. No fever.
Any vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass wind, or air or bits in your urine?
No, nothing like that.
Do you take any painkillers such as ibuprofen or codeine, or any other medicines?
model.why: NSAIDs and opioids: complication risk and constipation

model.text: Just paracetamol now and then.
And do you remember what the scan was: a CT, or a camera test into the bowel?
model.why: Clarifies whether the colon has been fully examined

model.text: I’m not sure what kind of scan it was. I don’t remember a camera test.
What have you been thinking this is, and is anything worrying you?
I assumed it’s the diverticular thing. I just want to know how to stop the pain and get my bowels back to normal.

Thank you. The out-of-hours doctor examined your tummy and checked your temperature and pulse three weeks ago, and that’s in your notes. I’d also like to offer you an internal examination at the surgery, with a chaperone, if you’re happy.
model.why: Recorded abdominal exam and obs; in-person DRE offered with chaperone and consent

model.text: (After the findings are read out) Is it all right?

That examination found your tummy soft with some mild tenderness low on the left, no lumps and no fever — and today you’ve no fever or constant pain. This fits diverticular disease: the pouches can cause crampy pain and irregular bowels. It isn’t diverticulitis, which is when a pouch becomes inflamed and causes constant pain and fever.

But I don’t want to put everything down to the pouches. At 62, a change in bowel habit is a reason to check for bowel cancer, even when diverticula have been seen. The first step is a simple home stool test called FIT, which looks for tiny amounts of blood. If it’s positive, I’ll refer you urgently for a camera test.
model.why: NICE NG12 and HTG690: FIT for change in bowel habit, explained proportionately

model.text: Cancer? I hadn’t even thought of that.

Most likely it’s the diverticular disease, but we don’t know that the inside of the bowel has been looked at directly, so the test is the safe thing to do. Even if the FIT is normal, if the symptoms continue I’d still want to look further.
model.why: Honest, proportionate; explains a normal FIT is not the end

model.text: I’ll also do blood tests: a blood count to check for anaemia, iron levels, inflammation markers and kidney function.
model.why: FBC and ferritin (IDA is another FIT criterion), CRP, U&E

model.text: For the symptoms: build up fibre gradually, with whole grains, fruit and vegetables, and drink plenty. A fibre supplement from the pharmacy can help both the constipation and the looseness. For the cramps, a medicine called an antispasmodic. Keep to paracetamol for pain and avoid anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen.
Will I need antibiotics?
Antibiotics don’t help diverticular disease without inflammation, and even mild diverticulitis often settles without them. They’re for when someone is unwell with infection.

Seek help the same day if the pain becomes constant or severe, you get a fever or shivers, bleed from the back passage, vomit, or can’t open your bowels or pass wind. I’ll ring you with the FIT and blood results, and see you in about four to six weeks to review. Can you tell me the plan?
The stool test and bloods, more fibre and water, the cramp medicine, no ibuprofen, and come back quickly if the pain is constant or I bleed or get a fever.
That’s it exactly.

social.t: Unpredictable bowels can restrict going out and working. Practical fibre changes need to fit her cooking and budget; increase gradually to limit bloating.
She has not mentioned cancer; introducing the FIT needs honest, proportionate language so she neither dismisses the test nor panics.

legal.t: Explain and seek consent for a rectal examination; offer a chaperone and record the offer and the name of the chaperone (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).

professional.t: Track FIT kits that are not returned and results that need action; practice systems should flag outstanding tests.
A prior diagnosis on a report is a common cause of delayed cancer diagnosis; re-check the history each time.

community.t: She is within the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme age range in England, but screening is for people without symptoms: symptomatic FIT is separate. Dietitian input if needed; bowel charities for information.

redFlags: Change in bowel habit at 62: FIT per NICE NG12 and HTG690; suspected cancer referral if 10 µg Hb/g or more
Rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, abdominal or rectal mass
Constant pain with fever, peritonism or sepsis features: acute or complicated diverticulitis, same-day assessment
Vomiting, distension, absolute constipation; pneumaturia; heavy rectal bleeding: admission
psychosocial: Assumes the old label explains everything
ice: Concern: the recurrent pain and erratic bowels
Expectation: a plan to control the symptoms

playbook.diagnosis: “This fits diverticular disease, but because your bowels have changed, I’d like a simple stool test to make sure nothing else is going on.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Diverticula are like little pockets pushed out through weak spots in the bowel wall, a bit like a worn inner tube. They can make the bowel cramp and behave unpredictably. If one gets inflamed, that’s diverticulitis, which is different.”

management.reflectIce: “You want the pain and your bowels sorted, and we’ll do that. Because your bowels have changed, I also want the stool test so we’re not assuming.”
management.psychosocial: Raise the cancer check honestly; make fibre changes gradual and practical.
sharedPlan: FIT now; suspected cancer referral if 10 µg Hb/g or more; further tests if symptoms persist despite a normal result
Gradual fibre increase with fluids; bulk-forming laxative; antispasmodic (doses per BNF)
Paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs and opioids; no antibiotics
safetyNet: Constant or severe pain, fever, rectal bleeding, vomiting, or unable to pass stool or wind: same-day assessment
Results by phone; review in four to six weeks

pitfalls.intro: The trap is the label on an old scan. Marks go to separating disease from diverticulitis, offering FIT for a change in bowel habit, managing symptoms per NG147, and safety-netting complications.

items.fail: Attributing the change in bowel habit to diverticular disease without FIT.
items.why: NICE NG12 and HTG690 recommend FIT for any adult with a change in bowel habit; cancer can mimic or coexist.
items.fix: Offer FIT and act on 10 µg Hb/g or more.

items.fail: Not asking what the previous scan was.
items.why: Diverticula on a CT do not mean the colon has been examined for a tumour.
items.fix: Check the report; plan colonic investigation if symptoms persist.

items.why: NG147: no antibiotics without acute diverticulitis, and a no-antibiotic strategy is often appropriate even then.
items.fix: Diet, bulk laxative and antispasmodic; antibiotics only when systemically unwell or high-risk.

items.fail: Recommending ibuprofen or codeine for pain.
items.why: NSAIDs and opioids may increase perforation risk and opioids worsen constipation.

items.fail: Ordering FIT without explaining why, or explaining it in alarming terms.
items.why: She expected a symptom plan; an unexplained or frightening test harms trust and uptake.
items.fix: Explain that a change in bowel habit at her age is checked routinely, and what happens with each result.

items.why: Diverticulitis and its complications need prompt recognition.
items.fix: List constant pain, fever, bleeding, vomiting and obstruction as same-day triggers; plan review.

timeMap.d: Let her explain; signal you’ll check for other causes.
Duration of bowel change; bleeding; weight loss; anaemia symptoms; pain pattern; fever; obstruction and fistula; NSAIDs, opioids; what the scan was.

Diverticular disease, not diverticulitis; FIT for change in bowel habit; bloods; fibre, fluids, bulk laxative, antispasmodic; no NSAIDs; no antibiotic.

wordPics.fail: Accepts ‘it’s the diverticular disease’, gives fibre advice and antibiotics, and does not offer FIT despite a change in bowel habit at 62.
wordPics.pass: Distinguishes disease from diverticulitis, offers FIT with a plan for urgent referral if positive, gives NG147 symptom management and safety-nets complications.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds out whether the colon was ever imaged, checks FBC and ferritin, explains that a normal FIT does not end the matter, advises against NSAIDs, withholds antibiotics with a clear reason, and raises the cancer check without alarming her.

avoid.dont: “The scan showed diverticular disease, so that explains it.”
avoid.instead: “It may well be the diverticula, but a change in your bowels at 62 needs a simple test to rule out anything else.”
avoid.why: NICE NG12 and HTG690 recommend FIT for any adult with a change in bowel habit; cancer can coexist.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you some antibiotics to settle it.”
avoid.instead: “Antibiotics don’t help diverticular disease; they’re for infection when someone is unwell.”
avoid.why: NG147: do not offer antibiotics for diverticular disease.

avoid.dont: “Take ibuprofen when the pain is bad.”
avoid.why: NG147 advises avoiding NSAIDs and opioids where possible because of perforation risk.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG147 Diverticular disease: diagnosis and management (2019) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE HTG690 Quantitative faecal immunochemical testing to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care · [4] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Diverticulosis is common and usually incidental; diverticular disease means symptoms from the diverticula; diverticulitis means inflammation. A 62-year-old with a change in bowel habit must not have it written off as diverticular disease: NICE NG12 and HTG690 [2, 3] recommend offering FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit, and a result of 10 µg Hb/g or more triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral. Manage the symptomatic disease with diet, fluids, bulk-forming laxatives and an antispasmodic [1]; recognise acute diverticulitis and its complications, and give clear safety-net advice.

points.t: Diverticulosis: pouches without symptoms, usually found incidentally. Diverticular disease: intermittent lower abdominal (usually left-sided) pain, often with altered bowel habit, bloating or mucus, without systemic inflammation. Acute diverticulitis: constant abdominal pain, usually left iliac fossa, with fever, localised tenderness and raised inflammatory markers; complicated if abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction or haemorrhage [1].

NG147 [1]: advise a healthy balanced diet with whole grains, fruit and vegetables, increasing fibre gradually with adequate fluids; consider a bulk-forming laxative for constipation and an antispasmodic for cramping; do not offer antibiotics for diverticular disease. Doses per BNF. Review NSAID and opioid use, which are linked to complications.

NG147 [1]: if systemically well without complications, consider a no-antibiotic strategy with advice to return if symptoms persist or worsen; offer an antibiotic (co-amoxiclav first choice, per NG147 and BNF) if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or with significant comorbidity. Advise paracetamol and avoidance of NSAIDs and opioids where possible, because they may increase the risk of perforation. Refer for same-day hospital assessment if pain is uncontrolled, a complication is suspected, fluids cannot be maintained, or the person is frail or cannot be managed at home.

NICE NG12 [2] and HTG690 [3]: offer FIT to adults with an abdominal mass, a change in bowel habit or iron-deficiency anaemia; to those aged 40 and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain; to those under 50 with rectal bleeding and unexplained abdominal pain or weight loss; to those aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss; and to those aged 60 and over with anaemia even without iron deficiency. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more. A rectal mass or unexplained anal mass or ulceration is referred without FIT. A normal FIT does not end the matter if symptoms persist.

Find out what the earlier scan was and whether the whole colon was examined. A CT that reported diverticula is not the same as a colonoscopy or CT colonography that excluded a tumour, and symptoms may have changed since.

Severe or generalised abdominal pain or peritonism, sepsis features [4], significant rectal bleeding, vomiting with distension and absolute constipation (obstruction), pneumaturia or faecal vaginal discharge (fistula), or failure to improve. These need same-day hospital assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; lets her give the story and her question.
Impact of unpredictable bowels and pain on daily life and going out.
Picks up that she is unsure what the scan was and that no camera test is remembered; ‘isn’t how my bowels used to be’ as a change in habit.
Idea (diverticular disease explains it), concern (the recurrent pain and erratic bowels), expectation (a management plan); raises the cancer check sensitively.
Recorded abdominal examination and obs; in-person DRE offered with chaperone; FIT, FBC, ferritin, CRP, U&E.
Diverticular disease versus diverticulitis, colorectal cancer, IBS-type symptoms, constipation.
Bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, obstruction, fistula, sepsis; NSAID and opioid use.
Symptomatic diverticular disease, with colorectal cancer to be excluded because of the change in habit.
FIT per NICE NG12 and HTG690 with suspected cancer referral if 10 or more; NG147 diet, bulk laxative, antispasmodic; no antibiotic.
Paracetamol, avoid NSAIDs; FBC and ferritin; clarifies previous imaging.
Same-day advice for diverticulitis or complications; results by phone; review in four to six weeks; teach-back.

social.t: Unpredictable bowels can restrict going out and working. Practical fibre changes need to fit her cooking and budget; increase gradually to limit bloating.
She has not mentioned cancer; introducing the FIT needs honest, proportionate language so she neither dismisses the test nor panics.

legal.t: Explain and seek consent for a rectal examination; offer a chaperone and record the offer and the name of the chaperone (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).

professional.t: Track FIT kits that are not returned and results that need action; practice systems should flag outstanding tests.
A prior diagnosis on a report is a common cause of delayed cancer diagnosis; re-check the history each time.

community.t: She is within the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme age range in England, but screening is for people without symptoms: symptomatic FIT is separate. Dietitian input if needed; bowel charities for information.

psychosocial: Assumes the old label explains everything
ice: Concern: the recurrent pain and erratic bowels

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This fits diverticular disease, but because your bowels have changed, I’d like a simple stool test to make sure nothing else is going on.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Diverticula are like little pockets pushed out through weak spots in the bowel wall, a bit like a worn inner tube. They can make the bowel cramp and behave unpredictably. If one gets inflamed, that’s diverticulitis, which is different.”

management.reflectIce: “You want the pain and your bowels sorted, and we’ll do that. Because your bowels have changed, I also want the stool test so we’re not assuming.”
management.psychosocial: Raise the cancer check honestly; make fibre changes gradual and practical.
sharedPlan: FIT now; suspected cancer referral if 10 µg Hb/g or more; further tests if symptoms persist despite a normal result
Gradual fibre increase with fluids; bulk-forming laxative; antispasmodic (doses per BNF)
Paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs and opioids; no antibiotics
safetyNet: Constant or severe pain, fever, rectal bleeding, vomiting, or unable to pass stool or wind: same-day assessment
Results by phone; review in four to six weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is the label on an old scan. Marks go to separating disease from diverticulitis, offering FIT for a change in bowel habit, managing symptoms per NG147, and safety-netting complications.

items.fail: Attributing the change in bowel habit to diverticular disease without FIT.
items.why: NICE NG12 and HTG690 recommend FIT for any adult with a change in bowel habit; cancer can mimic or coexist.
items.fix: Offer FIT and act on 10 µg Hb/g or more.

items.fail: Not asking what the previous scan was.
items.why: Diverticula on a CT do not mean the colon has been examined for a tumour.
items.fix: Check the report; plan colonic investigation if symptoms persist.

items.why: NG147: no antibiotics without acute diverticulitis, and a no-antibiotic strategy is often appropriate even then.
items.fix: Diet, bulk laxative and antispasmodic; antibiotics only when systemically unwell or high-risk.

items.fail: Recommending ibuprofen or codeine for pain.
items.why: NSAIDs and opioids may increase perforation risk and opioids worsen constipation.

items.fail: Ordering FIT without explaining why, or explaining it in alarming terms.
items.why: She expected a symptom plan; an unexplained or frightening test harms trust and uptake.
items.fix: Explain that a change in bowel habit at her age is checked routinely, and what happens with each result.

items.why: Diverticulitis and its complications need prompt recognition.
items.fix: List constant pain, fever, bleeding, vomiting and obstruction as same-day triggers; plan review.
